summaries.example: Imagine a doctor sends a blood sample to a lab. The lab checks chemicals in the blood. Another doctor studies one body part and chooses a medicine that was tested on many people. This shows several biomedical habits: looking for physical causes, using experiments, and studying body parts. These habits can help, but they may not tell the whole story of a person’s health.
summaries.summary: Biomedicine is the main framework used by many modern health institutions. It connects biology, medicine, laboratories, technology, hospitals, companies, and government programs. It commonly explains illness through physical and chemical processes, prefers carefully controlled experiments, and often studies bodies by looking at their smaller parts. These ideas have helped produce important treatments and technologies. Still, philosophers debate whether this approach pays enough attention to patients’ experiences, social lives, environments, and communities. They also ask who gets heard, how health and disease should be defined, and whether medical institutions sometimes expand too far into everyday life. The entry also describes other approaches, including humanistic medicine, population health, and traditional healing practices.
key_ideas: Biomedicine is more than a mix of biology and medicine. It is also a way of thinking, a history, and a worldwide set of institutions.
It often searches for physical causes of illness and values laboratory tests, technology, and controlled experiments.
Studying small body parts can be useful, but a person’s feelings, relationships, surroundings, and goals may also matter.
Philosophers ask whether biomedicine listens fairly to patients and whether health problems are sometimes treated as only individual responsibilities.
Other approaches, such as patient-centered care and population health, try to add personal stories or social conditions to the picture.
summaries.why_it_matters: Biomedicine affects how people are tested, diagnosed, treated, and taught about health. Understanding its ideas helps us notice both its strengths and its limits. It can encourage useful scientific testing while also reminding us that a patient is not just a collection of body parts. Fair health care may need physical evidence, careful listening, and attention to social conditions.

important_terms.definition: A large way of organizing ideas and practices. It helps people decide what questions to ask and what kinds of answers count as good answers.
A way of thinking about health that usually looks for physical, chemical, and biological causes and uses laboratory research and experiments.
The idea that something can be understood by studying its smaller parts. In biomedicine, this can mean studying cells, organs, or chemicals.
A person’s or group’s information and understanding. Philosophers ask whose knowledge is trusted in health care and whose may be ignored.
When everyday parts of life start being treated as medical problems that need medical attention.

questions_to_think_about: What can a blood test show, and what might it miss?
Should a patient’s own description of pain count as important evidence?
Can studying body parts help us understand the whole person?
Which health problems might be connected to homes, jobs, food, or neighborhoods?

summaries.example: Consider a new treatment for back pain. An evidence-based approach might compare two treatments in randomized controlled trials, combine results from several studies, and use the findings to create a guideline. Critics do not necessarily reject evidence. They ask whether the trials measure what matters to a particular patient, whether patient experience and clinical judgment have been undervalued, and whether laboratory or mechanistic evidence has been ranked too low. The disagreement concerns what evidence is best and how it should guide care.
summaries.summary: The entry examines biomedicine as a framework for organizing relations between biology and medicine, not merely as their overlap. It is also a post-World War II historical development and a global institutional system involving research, clinical practice, technology, industry, government, and health policy. Its central tendencies are to seek biological, chemical, and physical explanations; privilege laboratory and experimental methods; and explain complex conditions through bodily parts and processes. Philosophical analysis asks whether these tendencies amount to physicalism, reductionism, a Kuhnian paradigm, or something closer to a Lakatosian research programme, while avoiding commitment to one classification. Major debates concern the definitions of health and disease, the authority of randomized trials versus clinical expertise and mechanistic evidence, the difficulty of measuring well-being, and the place of patient experience. Critics also investigate epistemic injustice, medicalization, colonial power, surveillance, and unequal distribution. The entry presents alternatives that may reform, supplement, or challenge biomedicine, including humanistic, biopsychosocial, population-health, gentle, and traditional approaches.
key_ideas: Biomedicine is simultaneously an intellectual framework, a historical development, and a powerful global institution; these dimensions developed together.
Its characteristic commitments include restricting disease causes primarily to biological, chemical, and physical phenomena, emphasizing experimental methods, and using reductionist explanations.

The meaning of evidence is disputed inside biomedicine. Randomized controlled trials and meta-analyses are highly valued, while clinical expertise, mechanistic research, and patient testimony may receive different weight.

A naturalistic account may define disease through impaired typical functioning, but philosophers dispute how reference groups and standards of normality are chosen and what such definitions imply for action.
Institutional power matters: medical categories, technologies, and policies can distribute benefits and burdens, silence patient knowledge, or shift social problems onto individuals.

Alternative frameworks do not all reject biomedical science. Patient-centered care, the biopsychosocial model, population health, gentle medicine, and traditional practices propose different additions, limits, or standards.
summaries.why_it_matters: Biomedical institutions shape what counts as illness, evidence, expertise, and a successful treatment. Their methods have supported major health technologies and interventions, but their authority can also make some experiences or social causes harder to recognize. Philosophical scrutiny therefore matters for improving inquiry and care: it asks how scientific rigor can coexist with uncertainty, patient agency, diverse knowledge, and attention to the conditions in which people live.

important_terms.definition: A broad structure of ideas, methods, institutions, and assumptions that organizes research and practice. The entry treats biomedicine as a framework rather than assigning it one uncontested philosophical label.

The dominant approach linking contemporary biology and medicine, especially in many Western and global institutions. It emphasizes biological, chemical, and physical causes, experimentation, and analysis of bodily parts and processes.
The study of what exists or what kinds of things are real. In biomedicine, ontological questions concern bodies, disease, biological processes, and what may be excluded from medical explanation.

A view or method that explains a complex phenomenon through the properties and interactions of its parts. It can be a powerful research strategy, but critics argue it may overlook wholes, experiences, or social contexts.
The study of knowledge, evidence, expertise, and justified belief. Philosophers of biomedicine examine experiments, measurements, clinical judgment, and whose testimony is trusted.
A pattern in which someone is unfairly treated as less credible, or lacks shared concepts needed to understand and communicate their experience.

The process by which conditions or activities not previously treated as medical become defined as needing medical attention. It may be used descriptively, though over-medicalization is generally a criticism.
An approach that gives greater weight to the patient as a person, including agency, goals, experiences, and participation in decisions.

questions_to_think_about: If a randomized trial gives an average result, how should it guide treatment for one particular patient?
Can a disease be biologically real while its practical boundaries are shaped by social values and institutions?
When does focusing on genes or body parts clarify a problem, and when might it hide environmental or social causes?
What would count as fair treatment of a patient whose testimony conflicts with a standard test?
Can an alternative medical framework be evaluated without forcing it to adopt all biomedical standards?

summaries.example: Suppose a student has frequent headaches. A biomedical visit might involve tests for physical causes and a medicine supported by controlled studies. That can be helpful, but another student might ask about sleep, stress, food, school conditions, or what the student feels. The disagreement is not simply “science versus no science.” It is about which kinds of evidence should matter and whether a good explanation must include both the body and the person’s situation.
summaries.summary: Biomedicine is the main framework used by many contemporary medical and scientific institutions. The entry presents it as a changing historical development, a worldwide social institution, and a way of producing knowledge. It commonly explains disease through physical, chemical, and biological processes; relies heavily on laboratories, technology, and experiments; and uses reductionism, the strategy of explaining larger problems through smaller parts. These commitments have helped create powerful treatments and research tools. Philosophers nevertheless debate what counts as health or disease, whether controlled trials should outrank other evidence, how patient experience should enter decisions, and whether measurements can really be value-free. They also examine unfair treatment of patients as knowers, the expansion of medical authority into everyday life, and the unequal global effects of biomedical institutions. Proposed alternatives include humanistic and patient-centered care, biopsychosocial and population-health approaches, gentler treatment, and traditional healing frameworks.
key_ideas: Biomedicine is a system of ideas and organizations, not just a subject located between biology and medicine.
It often gives priority to physical causes, laboratory technology, controlled experiments, and explanations based on parts.
Evidence-based medicine creates guidelines from research, but experts disagree about how much weight to give trials, clinical experience, laboratory mechanisms, and patient knowledge.
Health and disease are not always easy to define or measure. Ideas about normal function can involve choices about comparison groups and standards.
Philosophers study how biomedical power affects patients, communities, global health systems, and the boundary between ordinary life and medical problems.
Alternative approaches may emphasize stories, mental and social factors, living conditions, cautious treatment, or traditional ideas of balance.
summaries.why_it_matters: The biomedical framework influences everyday decisions about testing, diagnosis, treatment, research funding, and public health. Learning about its assumptions makes it easier to ask whether a medical answer is scientifically supported, personally suitable, and socially fair. It also shows why improving health may require more than finding a physical cause: listening, uncertainty, living conditions, and power can matter too.

important_terms.definition: A broad plan for understanding a subject. It includes ideas, methods, and institutions that guide which questions are asked and which answers are accepted.

The dominant modern approach that connects biology with medicine. It usually explains illness through physical, chemical, and biological processes and values laboratory research and controlled testing.
A way of explaining something complex by focusing on its smaller parts. This may reveal useful causes, but it can leave out relationships among parts or the person’s wider life.
The study of how knowledge is made and supported. In health care, it includes questions about experiments, evidence, measurement, and professional expertise.
Unfair treatment of someone as a knower. For example, a patient may not be believed, or may lack the shared language needed to explain an illness.
When something that was not previously considered a medical condition becomes treated as one. Philosophers debate when this helps and when it intrudes too much into life.
A style of care that treats the patient as a person with experiences, choices, values, and a story, rather than only as a disease or body part.

questions_to_think_about: What kinds of evidence should a doctor use when treating one person?
Why might an average result from a study not fit every patient?
What could be lost when a whole person is described mainly through organs, cells, or chemicals?
How might a medical label help someone, and how might it create unfair treatment?
Should improving health focus mostly on hospitals and medicines, or also on housing, work, food, and neighborhoods?
